content: The following text provides a detailed overview of various studies, trials, and guidelines related to tuberculosis (TB) prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, particularly in populations at high risk, such as individuals living with HIV, children, and those exposed to multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). Below is a professional summary of the key points: 1. Symptom-Based TB Screening in HIV Patients: Ahmad Khan et al. (2014) evaluated the effectiveness of symptom-based TB screening among people living with HIV and found its performance to be suboptimal. This highlights the need for improved diagnostic tools in this population. 2. TB Screening in Pregnant Women: Calnan (2016) discussed strategies for TB screening in both HIV-infected and uninfected pregnant and postpartum women in Swaziland, emphasizing the importance of tailored approaches in high-risk groups. 3. WHO 4-Symptom Tool Evaluation: Hanifa et al. (2015) assessed the WHO 4-symptom screening tool for ruling out TB, using data from the X-PHACTOR study. The findings underscored the limitations of symptom-based screening in certain settings. 4. Undiagnosed TB in HIV Clinics: Kufa et al. (2012) explored the prevalence of undiagnosed TB among HIV clinic attendees and its association with antiretroviral therapy. The study emphasized the implications for intensified case finding, isoniazid preventive therapy, and infection control. 5. TB Case Finding in Pregnant Women in Kenya: LaCourse et al. (2016) reported poor performance of symptom screening and rapid diagnostic tests for TB in HIV-infected pregnant women, calling for better diagnostic strategies in this group. 6. Chest Radiography in TB Screening: Nguyen et al. (2016) highlighted the yield of chest radiography in TB screening for HIV-infected individuals at district-level clinics, demonstrating its utility as a diagnostic tool. 7. Isoniazid and Antiretroviral Therapy for TB Prevention: Rangaka et al. (2014) conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of isoniazid combined with antiretroviral therapy in preventing TB. The results supported the use of this combination in high-risk populations. 8. Symptom and Radiographic Screening in TB Prevalence Surveys: Den Boon et al. (2006) evaluated the effectiveness of symptom and chest radiographic screening in TB prevalence surveys, providing insights into their diagnostic value. 9. Nationwide TB Prevalence Surveys: Several studies, including those by Adetifa et al. (2012) in Gambia and Kapata et al. (2013–2014) in Zambia, reported on the prevalence of TB in various countries, offering critical data for TB control programs. 10. Latent TB Diagnosis in High-Risk Groups: Auguste et al. (2016) conducted a systematic review and economic evaluation of diagnostic methods for latent TB in children, immunocompromised individuals, and recent arrivals from high-incidence countries. 11. Comparison of TST and IGRA: Mahomed et al. (2011) compared the tuberculin skin test (TST) and Quantiferon-TB Gold in predicting TB disease in adolescents, while Sharma et al. (2017) evaluated these tests in high TB-burden settings. 12. Shorter Regimens for Latent TB Treatment: Studies by Menzies et al. (2018) and Sterling et al. (2011) compared shorter regimens, such as 4 months of rifampin or 3 months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, to the standard 9-month isoniazid regimen. These shorter regimens were found to be effective and associated with better adherence. 13. TB Prevention in Children Exposed to MDR-TB: The TB CHAMP and V-QUIN trials evaluated the efficacy and safety of levofloxacin as a preventive treatment for children exposed to MDR-TB. These studies assessed outcomes such as TB incidence, adverse events, and treatment adherence. 14. Safety of Fluoroquinolones: Studies, including those by Takizawa et al. (1999) and Hampel et al. (1997), examined the safety of fluoroquinolones, particularly in pediatric populations, and highlighted potential adverse effects such as arthropathy. 15. WHO Guidelines on TB Preventive Treatment: The WHO consolidated guidelines provide recommendations for TB preventive treatment, including the use of isoniazid, rifampin, and rifapentine in various populations, emphasizing the importance of tailored approaches based on individual risk factors. 16. Global TB Reports: The 2023 Global TB Report by WHO offers comprehensive data on TB incidence, prevalence, and control efforts worldwide, serving as a critical resource for policymakers and healthcare providers. These studies and guidelines collectively underscore the importance of evidence-based strategies for TB prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, particularly in high-risk populations such as those living with HIV, children, and individuals exposed to MDR-TB.
